subfield: Condensed matter and materials physics / photovoltaics
motivation: Miyasaka first used organometal halide perovskites as light absorbers in photovoltaic cells (2009). Park and Snaith (2012) independently turned them into stable solid-state devices, and Snaith showed that these materials work as true thin-film semiconductors with long carrier diffusion lengths. Their work started a new field. Certified efficiencies rose from about 4% to over 26% in single junctions and above 33% in perovskite-silicon tandems, a pace without precedent in photovoltaics. The discovery showed that solution-processed, defect-tolerant ionic semiconductors can match the optoelectronic quality of crystalline silicon. That has changed the physics of semiconductors, with consequences that reach LEDs, detectors and lasers. Synchrotron and neutron studies of their structure, ion migration and phase behaviour have become central to materials physics. The work has had broad impact across physics, chemistry and engineering, and it is now moving into industrial production for the energy transition.
